subject: math
title: Number Sense: Integers, Order of Operations, Fractions, and Decimals
objectives: Students will locate, compare, and order integers, fractions, and decimals on a number line.
Students will add, subtract, multiply, and divide positive and negative numbers using the sign rules.
Students will evaluate numerical expressions using the correct order of operations, including grouping symbols and absolute value.
Students will add, subtract, multiply, and divide fractions, mixed numbers, and decimals, and convert between fractions and decimals.
Students will solve multi-step real-world word problems involving money, temperature, and measurement.
teach:
Objectives

  • Locate, compare, and order integers, fractions, and decimals on a number line.
  • Compute with positive and negative numbers using the sign rules.
  • Evaluate expressions with the correct order of operations, including parentheses and absolute value bars.
  • Compute with fractions, mixed numbers, and decimals, and convert between them.
  • Solve multi-step word problems with money, temperature, and measurement.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen with a large number line from −10 to 10
  • Printed or digital copies of this week's Student Lesson and Study Sheet
  • Scratch paper and pencils (students will have an erasable note board on test day, so build the habit of writing every step)
  • An on-screen or handheld scientific calculator for the last part of the lesson only
  • Optional: fraction strips or a ruler marked in eighths for students who need a visual model

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Five quick problems that reveal what students remember about signs, fractions, and decimals.
Direct instruction20Number line and integers (6 min), order of operations (5 min), fractions (5 min), decimals and conversions (4 min). Model the worked examples.
Guided practice15Students work six problems in pairs or along with you; you circulate, check signs and steps.
Independent practice15Students start the 12 weekly practice items (items 1–8 in class; finish at home).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding, preview of the exit ticket, and this week's study plan.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Put these on the board as students arrive. Tell them not to worry about getting everything right; this is a check on what they remember, not a grade.

  1. −4 + 9
  2. 3 − 10
  3. 1/2 + 1/4
  4. 0.5 + 0.25
  5. Which is greater, −2 or −5?

Answers: (1) 5   (2) −7   (3) 3/4   (4) 0.75   (5) −2

Point out that problems 3 and 4 are the same quantity written two ways. That connection between fractions and decimals runs through the whole lesson. Problem 5 is the one most adults miss; use it to launch the number line.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

1. The number line and integers (about 6 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Integers are the whole numbers and their opposites: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …. Zero is neither positive nor negative.
  • On a number line, numbers increase to the right and decrease to the left. So −2 is greater than −5 because it is farther right. Use a real context: −2°F is warmer than −5°F.
  • Absolute value is distance from zero, so it is never negative: |−6| = 6 and |6| = 6. Absolute value bars also act as grouping symbols: work inside them first.
  • Adding and subtracting: adding a positive moves right; adding a negative moves left. Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite: 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8.
  • Multiplying and dividing: same signs give a positive result; different signs give a negative result. With several factors, count the negatives: an even number of negatives gives a positive product, an odd number gives a negative product.

Worked Example 1 (integers and absolute value). At 5 a.m. the temperature in a mountain town was −7°F. By 3 p.m. it was 12°F. How many degrees did the temperature rise?

Change = final − starting = 12 − (−7)

12 − (−7) = 12 + 7 = 19

Check with distance on the number line: from −7 up to 0 is 7 degrees, and from 0 up to 12 is 12 degrees. 7 + 12 = 19. The same answer comes from |12 − (−7)| = |19| = 19.

Answer: the temperature rose 19 degrees.

2. Order of operations (about 5 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Write the order on the board: Parentheses (and other grouping symbols, including absolute value bars and fraction bars) → Exponents → Multiplication and Division, left to right → Addition and Subtraction, left to right.
  • Stress the “left to right” part. The memory phrase PEMDAS makes many adults think multiplication always comes before division and addition always comes before subtraction. That is not true; they are partners, and you work them in the order they appear.
  • Have students rewrite the whole expression after every step. One step per line prevents most errors.

Worked Example 2 (order of operations). Evaluate 7 − 2 × (5 − 9) ÷ 4.

Parentheses first: 5 − 9 = −4, so the expression is 7 − 2 × (−4) ÷ 4

Multiply and divide left to right: 2 × (−4) = −8, so 7 − (−8) ÷ 4

−8 ÷ 4 = −2, so 7 − (−2)

Subtracting a negative: 7 − (−2) = 7 + 2 = 9

Answer: 9. Ask the class what happens if someone does 7 − 2 first (they get 5 × (−4) ÷ 4 = −5). That is the most common wrong answer.

3. Fractions and mixed numbers (about 5 minutes)

Talking points:

  • To add or subtract, you need a common denominator. Rewrite each fraction as an equivalent fraction, then add or subtract the numerators only. The denominator stays the same.
  • To multiply, multiply straight across: numerator times numerator, denominator times denominator. No common denominator needed.
  • To divide, keep the first fraction, change division to multiplication, and flip the second fraction (use its reciprocal).
  • With mixed numbers, convert to improper fractions first: 2 1/4 = (2 × 4 + 1)/4 = 9/4. Always simplify the final answer.

Worked Example 3 (fractions).

(a) Subtract: 3 1/2 − 1 2/3

Convert: 3 1/2 = 7/2 and 1 2/3 = 5/3

Common denominator 6: 7/2 = 21/6 and 5/3 = 10/6

21/6 − 10/6 = 11/6 = 1 5/6

(b) Divide: 3/4 ÷ 3/8

Keep, change, flip: 3/4 × 8/3 = 24/12 = 2

Sense check: 3/8 fits into 3/4 exactly twice, because 3/4 = 6/8.

Answers: (a) 1 5/6   (b) 2

4. Decimals and conversions (about 4 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Add and subtract decimals by lining up the decimal points. Fill empty places with zeros: 20 − 9.89 is 20.00 − 9.89.
  • Multiply as if there were no decimal points, then count the total number of decimal places in the two factors and place the decimal point that many places from the right.
  • Divide by a decimal by moving the decimal point in the divisor to make it a whole number, and move the decimal point in the dividend the same number of places.
  • A fraction is a division problem: 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375. To compare fractions and decimals, convert everything to decimals.

Worked Example 4 (decimals in context). Rosa buys 12.6 gallons of gas at $3.45 per gallon. What is the total cost?

Multiply 126 × 345 = 43,470

Decimal places: 12.6 has one, 3.45 has two, so the answer has three: 43.470

Check by breaking it apart: 12 × 3.45 = 41.40 and 0.6 × 3.45 = 2.07; 41.40 + 2.07 = 43.47

Answer: $43.47

Teacher note: If time is short, model Examples 2 and 3 fully and assign Example 4 as a think-aloud for a volunteer. Keep the calculator away until the last five minutes of independent practice so students strengthen mental and written computation; the GED's first section does not allow a calculator.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Work these with the class. Have students try each one for about two minutes, then call on someone to explain each step aloud while you write it.

  1. 12 + 8 ÷ 4 − 3 × 2
  2. −6 × (−3) − 5
  3. 2/3 + 3/4
  4. 4.2 ÷ 0.06
  5. |−8| − |2 − 6|
  6. Order from least to greatest: −1.2, −3/2, 0.8, 3/4

Answers with steps:

1. 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 3 × 2 = 6; then 12 + 2 − 6 = 8.

2. −6 × (−3) = 18 (same signs, positive); 18 − 5 = 13.

3. 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12; 8/12 + 9/12 = 17/12 = 1 5/12.

4. Move both decimal points two places: 420 ÷ 6 = 70.

5. |−8| = 8; inside the second bars, 2 − 6 = −4, and |−4| = 4; 8 − 4 = 4.

6. Convert: −3/2 = −1.5 and 3/4 = 0.75. Order: −3/2, −1.2, 3/4, 0.8.

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students open this week's 12 practice items and complete items 1–8 in class. Items 9–12 are the harder multi-step problems; students finish them at home. Circulate and look at scratch work, not just answers. If a student is stuck, ask “What does the problem tell you to do first?” before giving any hint.

Checks for Understanding

Use these quick questions during instruction and in the wrap-up. Students can answer on mini whiteboards, in the chat, or aloud.

  • Why is −10 less than −2? Expected: −10 is farther left on the number line (or: −10° is colder than −2°).
  • What is 15 − 3 × 4? Expected: 3 (multiply first: 15 − 12). Students who say 48 worked left to right.
  • Is (−2)(−3)(−1) positive or negative? Expected: negative, −6, because there are three negative factors (an odd number).
  • Write 3/8 as a decimal. Expected: 0.375 (3 ÷ 8).
  • What is 1/2 ÷ 1/4? Expected: 2 (1/2 × 4/1 = 2). Ask: “How many quarters are in a half dollar?”

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Working strictly left to right. In 18 − 6 ÷ 3, a student subtracts first and gets 4. Correction: circle every multiplication and division sign first and do those, then add and subtract. Correct answer: 18 − 2 = 16.

Always multiplying before dividing. In 24 ÷ 4 × 3, a student does 4 × 3 = 12 and gets 2. Correction: multiplication and division are partners worked left to right: 24 ÷ 4 = 6, then 6 × 3 = 18.

Sign errors with subtraction. Students write 5 − (−3) = 2. Correction: rewrite every subtraction as adding the opposite before computing: 5 + 3 = 8.

Adding denominators. Students write 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5. Correction: show with a picture or money that half a dollar plus a third of a dollar is more than half, so 2/5 cannot be right. Use a common denominator: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

Misplacing the decimal point. Students compute 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.6. Correction: count decimal places (one + one = two), so 3 × 2 = 6 becomes 0.06. Estimate as a check: a little less than half of 0.3 is reasonable.

Splitting absolute value across subtraction. Students treat |3 − 11| as |3| − |11| or as 3 + 11. Correction: absolute value bars are grouping symbols. Compute inside first: 3 − 11 = −8, and |−8| = 8.

Differentiation

Support: Give students a printed number line from −20 to 20 and let them count jumps for every integer problem. Use money for decimals (0.25 is a quarter) and measuring cups or a ruler for fractions. Reduce multi-step problems to one step at a time and have the student rewrite the expression after each step. Allow a list of common fraction-decimal pairs (from the Study Sheet) during practice.

Stretch: Offer nested grouping and mixed forms. Example: evaluate [(−3)(4) + 18] ÷ (−2) − |−5|. Steps: (−3)(4) = −12; −12 + 18 = 6; 6 ÷ (−2) = −3; |−5| = 5; −3 − 5 = −8. Then ask these students to write their own word problem whose answer is −8 and trade with a partner.

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Ask two or three of the checks for understanding above. Then have each student say or type one rule they will remember (for example, “subtracting a negative means adding”). Preview the Post Lesson exit ticket and this week's study plan, including the weekly practice GED.

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • No-calculator questions. The math test opens with a short section where the calculator is not available. Number sense skills (signs, order of operations, fractions) appear there often.
  • Question formats. Multiple choice with four options; fill-in-the-blank (type a number); drop-down menus (choose “is less than,” “is greater than,” or “is equal to”); drag-and-drop (order numbers or sort expressions).
  • Typical wording. “What is the value of the expression?” “Which list shows the numbers in order from least to greatest?” “What was the temperature at 11 p.m.?” “How much change should she receive?”
  • Built-in traps. Wrong answer choices usually come from the exact mistakes listed above: left-to-right errors, sign errors, and decimal-point errors. Teach students to expect that a wrong answer will be on the list, so they must check their work rather than trust that a matching choice means they are right.
  • Real contexts. Money, temperatures, elevations above and below sea level, recipes, and measurements. These number skills are also the foundation for every later topic: ratios, percents, algebra, and geometry all depend on them.
student:
Welcome to Week 1

Every part of the GED math test depends on the skills in this lesson: working with negative numbers, doing steps in the right order, and handling fractions and decimals. If it has been a while since you did this kind of math, that is completely normal. Read each section, study the worked examples, and then try the problems yourself. Write every step on paper.

1. Integers and the Number Line

Integers are whole numbers and their opposites: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …. On a number line, numbers get bigger as you move right and smaller as you move left.

Key idea: A negative number with a bigger digit is actually smaller. −9 is less than −4, just as −9°F is colder than −4°F.

Absolute value means distance from zero. Distance is never negative, so |−7| = 7 and |7| = 7.

Adding and subtracting integers

  • Same signs: add the numbers and keep the sign. −5 + (−3) = −8.
  • Different signs: subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger one, and keep the sign of the number with the larger absolute value. −9 + 4 = −5.
  • Subtracting: change it to adding the opposite. 6 − (−2) = 6 + 2 = 8.

Multiplying and dividing integers

  • Same signs give a positive answer: (−4)(−5) = 20.
  • Different signs give a negative answer: −24 ÷ 6 = −4.

Example 1. Find −8 − (−3).

Change subtraction to adding the opposite: −8 + 3

Different signs: 8 − 3 = 5, and the larger absolute value (8) is negative.

Answer: −5

2. Order of Operations

When an expression has more than one operation, everyone must do the steps in the same order so they get the same answer.

  1. Grouping symbols: parentheses ( ), brackets [ ], and absolute value bars | |. Work inside them first.
  2. Exponents (you will study these in Week 3).
  3. Multiplication and division, from left to right, whichever comes first.
  4. Addition and subtraction, from left to right, whichever comes first.

Watch out: Multiplication does not always come before division, and addition does not always come before subtraction. They are partners. Work them in the order they appear, left to right.

Example 2. Evaluate 30 − 12 ÷ 3 × 2.

No grouping symbols. Multiply and divide from left to right.

12 ÷ 3 = 4, so 30 − 4 × 2

4 × 2 = 8, so 30 − 8

30 − 8 = 22

Answer: 22

3. Fractions

A fraction has a numerator (top) and a denominator (bottom). A mixed number like 2 1/4 has a whole part and a fraction part. Change it to an improper fraction before you compute: multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the denominator. 2 1/4 = (2 × 4 + 1)/4 = 9/4.

  • Add or subtract: find a common denominator, then add or subtract the numerators. The denominator stays the same.
  • Multiply: multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators.
  • Divide: keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, and flip the second fraction.
  • Simplify your answer by dividing the top and bottom by the same number.

Example 3.

(a) 2/5 + 1/3. The common denominator is 15.

2/5 = 6/15 and 1/3 = 5/15

6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15

(b) 5/6 ÷ 2/3. Keep, change, flip.

5/6 × 3/2 = 15/12

Simplify by dividing top and bottom by 3: 15/12 = 5/4 = 1 1/4

Answers: (a) 11/15   (b) 1 1/4

4. Decimals

  • Add or subtract: line up the decimal points. Add zeros if needed: 20 − 9.89 becomes 20.00 − 9.89 = 10.11.
  • Multiply: multiply as if there were no decimal points. Count the decimal places in both numbers together, and put that many places in the answer.
  • Divide by a decimal: move the decimal point in the number you are dividing by until it is a whole number, and move the other decimal point the same number of places.

Example 4.

(a) 1.25 × 2.4. Multiply 125 × 24 = 3,000. There are 2 + 1 = 3 decimal places, so the answer is 3.000, which is 3.

(b) 3.6 ÷ 0.12. Move both decimal points two places right: 360 ÷ 12 = 30.

Answers: (a) 3   (b) 30

5. Comparing Fractions and Decimals

To change a fraction into a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator: 5/8 = 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625. To put a mix of fractions and decimals in order, change them all to decimals first, then place them on a number line.

Strategy: Memorize a few common pairs: 1/2 = 0.5, 1/4 = 0.25, 3/4 = 0.75, 1/5 = 0.2, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/3 ≈ 0.333, 2/3 ≈ 0.667. They save time on the GED.

Example 5. Which is greater, −3/5 or −0.5?

−3/5 = −0.6. On the number line, −0.5 is to the right of −0.6.

Answer: −0.5 is greater.

Try It

Work each problem on paper, then check your answer.

1. −9 + 4

Show answer

Different signs: 9 − 4 = 5. The larger absolute value is 9, which is negative, so the answer is −5.

2. 24 ÷ 4 × 3 − 5

Show answer

Left to right: 24 ÷ 4 = 6; 6 × 3 = 18; 18 − 5 = 13.

3. 1 3/4 + 2 2/3

Show answer

1 3/4 = 7/4 and 2 2/3 = 8/3. Common denominator 12: 21/12 + 32/12 = 53/12 = 4 5/12.

4. 6.5 × 0.4

Show answer

65 × 4 = 260. Two decimal places in all: 2.60 = 2.6.

5. Order from least to greatest: 0.6, −0.65, 5/8, −2/3

Show answer

Convert: 5/8 = 0.625 and −2/3 ≈ −0.667. Order: −2/3, −0.65, 0.6, 5/8.
post:
Summary of Key Points

  • On a number line, numbers increase to the right. Among negative numbers, the one closer to zero is greater.
  • Absolute value is distance from zero and is never negative.
  • Subtracting a number means adding its opposite: a − (−b) = a + b.
  • Multiplying or dividing: same signs give a positive answer; different signs give a negative answer.
  • Order of operations: grouping symbols, exponents, multiplication and division (left to right), addition and subtraction (left to right).
  • Fractions need a common denominator to add or subtract; multiply straight across; to divide, multiply by the reciprocal.
  • Line up decimal points to add or subtract; count decimal places to multiply.
  • To compare fractions and decimals, change them all to decimals.

Exit Ticket

1. −5 − 7

Show answer

−5 + (−7) = −12

2. 10 − 2 × 3 + 4

Show answer

2 × 3 = 6; 10 − 6 = 4; 4 + 4 = 8

3. 3/4 − 1/6

Show answer

Common denominator 12: 9/12 − 2/12 = 7/12

4. 0.3 × 0.2

Show answer

3 × 2 = 6, with two decimal places: 0.06

5. Which is greater: −3/5 or −0.5?

Show answer

−3/5 = −0.6, and −0.5 is to its right on the number line, so −0.5 is greater.

Reflection

  • Which skill from this lesson felt most comfortable, and which one do you need to practice more?
  • Look back at a problem you got wrong. Was the mistake a sign error, an order-of-operations error, or a fraction or decimal error? What will you do differently next time?
  • Where do you use negative numbers, fractions, or decimals in your everyday life (money, cooking, work, weather)?

This Week's Study Plan

DayWhat to doTime
Day 1Reread sections 1 and 2 of the Student Lesson. Redo Examples 1 and 2 without looking, then check.20–30 min
Day 2Reread sections 3 and 4. Redo Examples 3 and 4. Rework the Try It problems.25–30 min
Day 3Complete all 12 weekly practice items. Read every explanation, even for the ones you got right.30–40 min
Day 4Study the vocabulary and the Study Sheet. Write five problems of your own (one for each skill) and solve them.20–30 min
Day 5Redo any practice items you missed. Make a list of your most common mistakes.20–30 min
Day 6Take this week's practice GED for Mathematical Reasoning under timed conditions. Set aside about two hours in a quiet place.About 2 hours
Day 7Review your practice GED results. Note which questions came from number sense and which came from topics still ahead.20–30 min

Test-taking strategy: check the signs before you choose. On the GED, the wrong answer choices are often the answers people get when they make a common mistake, especially a sign error. Before you pick an answer, ask yourself: “Should this answer be positive or negative? About how big should it be?” A quick estimate, such as “the temperature went down more than it went up, so the answer should be below where it started,” lets you catch an error before it costs you a point.

vocab.example: −3 is to the left of 1, so −3 < 1.

vocab.def: The number the same distance from zero on the other side of zero.

notes:
Week 1 Study Sheet: Number Sense

Integer Sign Rules

OperationRuleExample
Add, same signsAdd; keep the sign−5 + (−3) = −8
Add, different signsSubtract; keep sign of larger absolute value−9 + 4 = −5
SubtractAdd the opposite6 − (−2) = 8
Multiply/divide, same signsPositive(−4)(−5) = 20
Multiply/divide, different signsNegative−24 ÷ 6 = −4

Absolute value = distance from 0: |−7| = 7.

Order of Operations

  1. Grouping: ( ), [ ], | |, fraction bars
  2. Exponents
  3. Multiply and divide, left to right
  4. Add and subtract, left to right

Example: 30 − 12 ÷ 3 × 2 = 30 − 4 × 2 = 30 − 8 = 22

Fractions

  • Add/subtract: common denominator, then combine numerators.
  • Multiply: top × top, bottom × bottom.
  • Divide: keep, change, flip.
  • Mixed to improper: 2 1/4 = (2 × 4 + 1)/4 = 9/4.
  • Always simplify.

Decimals

  • Add/subtract: line up decimal points.
  • Multiply: count total decimal places.
  • Divide: make the divisor a whole number; move both points the same way.
  • Fraction to decimal: top ÷ bottom.

Common Fraction-Decimal Pairs

1/21/43/41/51/83/81/32/31/10
0.50.250.750.20.1250.375≈ 0.333≈ 0.6670.1

Top mistakes: working only left to right; 5 − (−3) is 8, not 2; never add denominators; count decimal places when multiplying; work inside absolute value bars first.

items.prompt:
The table shows the low temperatures in four towns on the same winter morning.

TownLow temperature (°F)
Hillcrest−8
Maple Falls−3
Riverton2
Pine Ridge−12

Which town had the coldest low temperature?
items.hint: The coldest temperature is the least number. Picture where each number sits on a number line.
items.explain:
The coldest temperature is the least number, which is the one farthest to the left on a number line.

Order from least to greatest: −12, −8, −3, 2.

−12°F is the least, so Pine Ridge was coldest.

Maple Falls (−3°F) is a common wrong choice: 3 is a small digit, but −3 is close to zero, so it is actually the warmest of the negative temperatures.

items.prompt:
What is the value of the expression below?

18 − 6 ÷ 3 × 2 + 1
items.hint: Do multiplication and division first, from left to right. Then add and subtract from left to right.
items.explain:
Multiply and divide first, from left to right:

6 ÷ 3 = 2, so the expression is 18 − 2 × 2 + 1

2 × 2 = 4, so 18 − 4 + 1

Then add and subtract from left to right:

18 − 4 = 14; 14 + 1 = 15

The choice 9 comes from working strictly left to right (18 − 6 = 12, 12 ÷ 3 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 8 + 1 = 9). The choice 18 comes from multiplying 3 × 2 before dividing.

items.prompt:
What is the value of the expression below?

|3 − 11| + |−5|
items.hint: Absolute value bars act like parentheses. Compute inside them first, then take the distance from zero.
items.explain:
Work inside the first set of bars: 3 − 11 = −8

|−8| = 8 and |−5| = 5

8 + 5 = 13

A common mistake is to write |3 − 11| as 3 + 11 = 14, which gives 19. Always compute inside the bars first.

items.prompt: Marisol buys a sandwich for $6.75, a drink for $1.89, and a bag of chips for $1.25. There is no tax. She pays with a $20 bill. How much change should she receive?
items.hint: First find the total cost. Then subtract it from $20.00, lining up the decimal points.
items.explain:
Add the costs, lining up the decimal points:

$6.75 + $1.89 = $8.64

$8.64 + $1.25 = $9.89

Subtract from the amount paid: $20.00 − $9.89 = $10.11

$9.89 is the total cost, not the change. $11.11 comes from a borrowing error in the subtraction.

items.prompt: At 6 a.m. the temperature in a city was −14°F. By 2 p.m. the temperature had risen 23 degrees. By 11 p.m. it had dropped 17 degrees from the 2 p.m. temperature. What was the temperature at 11 p.m.?
items.hint: A rise means add; a drop means subtract. Start at −14.
items.explain:
Start at −14. A rise of 23 degrees means add 23:

−14 + 23 = 9 (the 2 p.m. temperature was 9°F)

A drop of 17 degrees means subtract 17:

9 − 17 = −8

The temperature at 11 p.m. was −8°F.

8°F is a sign error. −54°F comes from subtracting both changes (−14 − 23 − 17). 20°F comes from starting at positive 14 (14 + 23 − 17).

items.prompt: Drag each number into its position so the numbers are in order from least (1st) to greatest (4th).
items.hint: Change the fractions to decimals first. Remember that among negative numbers, the one farther from zero is less.
items.explain:
Convert the fractions to decimals:

−3/4 = −0.75 and 2/5 = 0.4

Now compare −0.6, −0.75, 0.4, and 0.35.

The negatives come first. −0.75 is farther from zero than −0.6, so −0.75 is less.

Among the positives, 0.35 < 0.40.

Order: −3/4, −0.6, 0.35, 2/5

A common mistake is placing −0.6 first because 0.6 “looks” close to 0.75, or placing 0.35 last because 35 is bigger than 4.

items.prompt:
Choose the phrase that makes each statement true.

−2/3 {{0}} −0.6

|−5| {{1}} |3|

−(−4) {{2}} 4
items.hint: Convert −2/3 to a decimal. Absolute value is distance from zero. The opposite of a negative number is positive.
items.explain:
First statement: −2/3 ≈ −0.667. On a number line, −0.667 is to the left of −0.6, so −2/3 is less than −0.6.

Second statement: |−5| = 5 and |3| = 3. Since 5 > 3, |−5| is greater than |3|.

Third statement: −(−4) means the opposite of −4, which is 4. So −(−4) is equal to 4.

Choosing “is greater than” in the first statement is the common mistake: 2/3 is greater than 0.6, but for negative numbers the order flips.

items.prompt: Select two expressions that have a value of −6.
items.hint: Use the sign rules: same signs multiply or divide to a positive; different signs give a negative.
items.explain:
Evaluate each expression:

  • −2 × 3 = −6 (different signs, negative) Correct
  • −12 ÷ (−2) = 6 (same signs, positive)
  • 4 − 10 = −6 Correct
  • |−4 − 2| = |−6| = 6 (absolute value is never negative)
  • −9 + (−3) = −12
  • (−2)(−3) = 6 (same signs, positive)

The two expressions equal to −6 are −2 × 3 and 4 − 10.

items.prompt: A bread recipe calls for 2 1/4 cups of flour. Dana wants to make 2/3 of the recipe. How many cups of flour does she need?
items.hint: “2/3 of” means multiply by 2/3. Change the mixed number to an improper fraction first.
items.explain:
“2/3 of the recipe” means multiply the amount by 2/3.

Change the mixed number to an improper fraction: 2 1/4 = (2 × 4 + 1)/4 = 9/4

Multiply: 9/4 × 2/3 = 18/12

Simplify: 18/12 = 3/2 = 1 1/2 cups

3 3/8 comes from dividing by 2/3 instead of multiplying. 1 7/12 comes from subtracting 2/3. 2 1/6 comes from multiplying only the fraction part (1/4 × 2/3 = 1/6) and keeping the 2.

items.prompt:
What is the value of the expression below?

20 − 4(3 − 8) ÷ 2
items.hint: Start inside the parentheses. A number written right next to parentheses means multiply.
items.explain:
Parentheses first: 3 − 8 = −5, so the expression is 20 − 4(−5) ÷ 2

Multiply and divide from left to right:

4(−5) = −20, so 20 − (−20) ÷ 2

−20 ÷ 2 = −10, so 20 − (−10)

Subtracting a negative means adding: 20 + 10 = 30

The choice 10 comes from a sign error (20 − 10). The choice −40 comes from subtracting 20 − 4 first: 16 × (−5) ÷ 2 = −40.

items.prompt:
A carpenter has a board that is 8 3/4 feet long. She cuts off three pieces, and each piece is 1 5/6 feet long. Ignore the width of the saw cuts. How many feet of the board are left?

Enter your answer as a decimal or as an improper fraction.
items.hint: First find the total length of the three pieces. Then subtract that from 8 3/4.
items.explain:
Change the mixed numbers to improper fractions:

1 5/6 = (1 × 6 + 5)/6 = 11/6 and 8 3/4 = (8 × 4 + 3)/4 = 35/4

Total cut off: 3 × 11/6 = 33/6 = 11/2 = 5 1/2 feet

Subtract with a common denominator of 4: 35/4 − 22/4 = 13/4

13/4 = 3 1/4 = 3.25 feet

If you subtract only one piece (8 3/4 − 1 5/6), you get 6 11/12 feet, which is not what the question asks.

items.prompt: Jordan earns $18.40 per hour. Last week he worked 32 1/2 hours. His employer withholds 1/4 of his pay for taxes and other deductions. How much is Jordan's take-home pay for the week?
items.hint: Find his total pay first. If 1/4 is withheld, what fraction does he keep?
items.explain:
Total pay: 32 1/2 hours = 32.5 hours

$18.40 × 32.5:

$18.40 × 32 = $588.80 and $18.40 × 0.5 = $9.20

$588.80 + $9.20 = $598.00

If 1/4 is withheld, Jordan keeps 1 − 1/4 = 3/4 of his pay:

3/4 × $598.00 = $598.00 ÷ 4 × 3 = $149.50 × 3 = $448.50

$149.50 is the amount withheld, not the amount he keeps. $598.00 is his pay before deductions. $441.60 comes from leaving out the half hour (using 32 hours instead of 32.5).
